newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan pork export ban may reduce economic growth.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan pork export ban may reduce economic growth.

text.p: Taiwan officials said on Saturday the government's ban on pork exports because of an outbreak of hog foot-and-mouth disease may cause a fall in the island's economic growth in 1997.

"If it becomes definite that there will no pork exports this year, the influence (on economic growth) will reveal itself," Chan Teh-sung, statistics director of the economics ministry, told the state-run Central News Agency.
Chan said the value of pork exports in 1996, which stood at T$43.6 billion (US$1.55 billion), comprised 0.5 percent of Taiwan's total gross domestic product (GDP) for the year.
But he said the ministry had no immediate plans to revise its current GDP forecast of 6.28 percent for 1997.
"Right now we have to observe how events unfold before making any decisions," Chan said.

Taiwan on Thursday announced it would ban exports of all fresh and frozen pork products following an outbreak of the deadly and contagious foot-and-mouth disease, spelling huge losses for exporters and farmers.
The government said on Saturday it had begun to slaughter infected hogs and had set up a task force to monitor the situation.
President Lee Teng-hui announced the government would offer up to T$10 billion (US$360 million) in low-interest loans to pork processing companies to help defray losses.
Analysts told Reuters on Friday that the impact of the outbreak would be minor because the pork industry was a marginal export sector.
The industry's 1996 export value was 1.3 percent of Taiwan's overall exports, which stood at US$116.1 billion.
Japan, which receives more than 99 percent of Taiwan's pork exports, and South Korea said on Friday they had banned pork imports from Taiwan indefinitely because of the disease.
